passages.title: The built heaven, spread earth, and the call to flee to Allah
passages.tafsir:
These five ayat take you outside, look up, look down, look around — and then tell you to run. Allah points to the roof of the sky, the floor of the earth, and the pairedness woven through everything He has made; and the moment the evidence has landed, it turns into a single urgent command: **flee to Allah**, and do not set up another god beside Him.

What holds the passage together is that movement from *proof* to *response*. Ayat 47–49 are evidence. Ayat 50–51 are what a person with a working heart does about it.

## Where we are in the sūrah

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān sets the scene: the verses just before this spoke of the reality of the Hereafter and the Judgment Day, and of the punishment of those who denied that reality. So this passage arrives as reinforcement. It reaffirms the perfect power of Allah, reminds us of the reality of the Day of Resurrection, allays the doubt and suspicion of those who deny it, proves the oneness of Allah, and reiterates emphatically the duty to believe in the Messenger ﷺ.

That is worth holding onto, because it explains why the argument runs the way it does. A person who cannot believe the dead will be raised is being shown the sky over his head. Ibn Kathir opens his comment on these ayat with a heading that says it plainly: *proofs of Allah's Oneness abound in the creation of the heavens and the earth.* Allah, he writes, is reminding us of the creating of the higher and the lower worlds.

## Ayah 47 — the roof that does not fall

> **وَٱلسَّمَآءَ بَنَيۡنَٰهَا بِأَيۡيْدٖ وَإِنَّا لَمُوسِعُونَ**
> "With Hands We constructed the heaven. Verily, We are able to expand the vastness of space thereof." (as rendered in the translation of Ibn Kathir)

**"We constructed the heaven."** Ibn Kathir unpacks it: *We made it as a high roof, protected from falling.* Notice how much comfort is packed into that. Every roof a human being has ever built is a roof that can come down. This one was raised by a Builder whose work is protected from falling — you have lived your whole life under it without once bracing for it.

**"With *aydin*."** This is the phrase readers stop at. In the translation of Ibn Kathir's commentary it is rendered "with Hands", and he immediately reports the meaning given by the early authorities: *bi-aydin* here means **with strength**. He names them — ʿAbdullāh bin ʿAbbās, Mujāhid, Qatādah, Ath-Thawrī, "and several others." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān gives exactly the same reading: the word *aydin*, according to Sayyidnā Ibn ʿAbbās, means strength or power in this context, so the ayah reads "And the sky was built by Us with might." So the ayah's point is power: the sheer force that raised something that immense.

**"And We are certainly *la-mūsiʿūn*."** Ibn Kathir explains: *We made it vast and We brought its roof higher without pillars to support it, and thus it is hanging independently.* Maʿārif ul Qurʼān renders the phrase "and indeed, We are the One who expands." Two things are being said at once — vastness, and the ongoing capacity of the One who made it that vast. Take the image seriously for a moment: a ceiling with nothing under it. No columns. No scaffolding. It hangs independently, held by nothing you can see, which is to say held by Him.

And that is the argument against the deniers. A person who says raising the dead is impossible has just been asked to look at a roof that hangs on nothing.

## Ayah 48 — the floor that was smoothed for you

> **وَٱلۡأَرۡضَ فَرَشۡنَٰهَا فَنِعۡمَ ٱلۡمَٰهِدُونَ**
> "And We have made the earth a Firash; how excellent a spreader (thereof) are We!"

If ayah 47 is the roof, ayah 48 is the floor, and the pairing is deliberate — Ibn Kathir has just told us that Allah is reminding us of the higher and the lower worlds, named one after the other.

**"We made it a *firāsh*."** Ibn Kathir glosses *firāsh* as **a resting place for the created** — the earth as something laid down for you, the way a mat is spread out for someone to rest on. You are not clinging to the planet. You are resting on it.

**"How excellent a spreader are We!"** — *fa-niʿma al-māhidūn*. Ibn Kathir: *We spread it for its inhabitants.* Allah is not merely reporting that He did this; the wording carries praise for how well it was done. The earth is not a bare fact you happen to stand on. It is a hospitality — spread, laid out, made liveable, for creatures who did not ask for it and mostly do not notice it.

Between ayat 47 and 48 you have the whole of the world a human being inhabits, described in the language of a house: a raised roof and a spread floor, both of them built, both of them for you.

## Ayah 49 — everything comes in twos

> **وَمِن كُلِّ شَيۡءٍ خَلَقۡنَا زَوۡجَيۡنِ لَعَلَّكُمۡ تَذَكَّرُونَ**
> "And of everything We have created pairs, that you may remember."

*Zawjayn* — two of a pair. And Ibn Kathir refuses to let the reader shrink this to biology. **All the created are in pairs**, he says, and he walks through them: the heaven and earth; night and day; sun and moon; land and sea; light and darkness; faith and disbelief; death and life; misery and happiness; Paradise and Fire — and then, in addition to all of that, the animals and the plants.

Look at what that list does. It moves from the physical (heaven/earth, sun/moon) through the experiential (night/day, light/darkness) into the moral and the eternal (faith/disbelief, Paradise/Fire). Pairedness is not a curiosity of nature; on Ibn Kathir's reading it runs through every level of existence.

**And the conclusion Allah wants you to draw from it** is stated in the ayah itself: *laʿallakum tadhakkarūn* — "that you may remember." Remember what? Ibn Kathir spells it out: **and know that the Creator, Allah, is One without partners.** That is the logic. Everything in the creation is in pairs; the Creator alone is not. He stands outside the pattern He wove through everything else. The universe is full of twos precisely so that you will know the One.

Note also the wording: not "that you may learn" but *that you may remember* — the language of being reminded, of becoming mindful, as the translation of the ayah has it.

## Ayah 50 — the command the whole passage was building towards

> **فَفِرُّوٓاْ إِلَى ٱللَّهِۖ إِنِّي لَكُم مِّنۡهُ نَذِيرٞ مُّبِينٞ**
> "So, flee to Allah. Verily, I am a plain warner to you from Him."

Everything before this was evidence. Now comes the verdict, and it arrives with *fa-* — "so", "therefore". The sky, the earth, the pairs — **therefore run.**

**Why "flee" and not "come"?** The word chosen is the word of someone running *away* from danger, and that is the emotional truth of the command. This is not a polite invitation to draw nearer at your convenience. And the remarkable thing is where the fleeing goes: normally you flee *from* something *to* safety somewhere else — here, as the commentators read it, you flee from your own ruin to Allah Himself. There is no other direction. There is nowhere else that counts as away.

The commentators open this out in two complementary directions, and both are worth taking:

**Ibn Kathir:** *"So, flee to Allah" means — seek shelter with Him and trust in Him in all of your affairs.* This is the broad reading. Every matter of your life, without exception, gets handed to Him. Shelter and reliance, as a permanent posture.

**Sayyidnā Ibn ʿAbbās**, as Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reports him (citing Qurtubī): *"It means: Flee from your sins and take shelter in Allah for repentance."* This is the sharp, personal reading. The thing you are running from is named — it is your own sin — and the door you are running through is named too: repentance. A man fleeing his sins has only one place to go, and it is to the One he sinned against.

**Abu Bakr Warrāq and Junaid Baghdādī**, also cited there, complete the picture: the base self of a man and the devil invite him to commit sins, and they deceive him; he needs to take refuge in Allah, who will protect him against their evil. So the danger is not only behind you in the past; it is beside you, in your own lower self and in the invitation of the enemy, both of them working by deception. That is why the response has to be *flight* — you do not negotiate with a deceiver, you get away from him.

**"Verily, I am a plain warner to you from Him."** The Prophet ﷺ is the one instructed to say this — the translation makes the address explicit: *proclaim, O Prophet*. A **plain** warner: nothing veiled or coded about the warning. And *minhu*, "from Him": his authority is not his own, he is sent. The command to flee is not one man's advice; it is a summons delivered on behalf of the One you are being told to flee to.

## Ayah 51 — and do not set up another

> **وَلَا تَجۡعَلُواْ مَعَ ٱللَّهِ إِلَٰهًا ءَاخَرَۖ إِنِّي لَكُم مِّنۡهُ نَذِيرٞ مُّبِينٞ**
> "And set not up any other god along with Allah. Verily, I am a plain warner to you from Him."

Ibn Kathir's gloss is one line: *do not associate any partners with Him.*

Two observations on the shape of it. First, this ayah is the exact negative of ayah 50 — flee **to** Allah, and set up no other god **along with** Allah. Running to Him means running to Him alone; a refuge you share with rivals is not a refuge. Together they are the positive turning towards Allah and the clearing away of everything else — which is just what ayah 49 asked you to remember: that the Creator, Allah, is One without partners.

Second, the warner's sentence is repeated word for word: *"Verily, I am a plain warner to you from Him."* It closes ayah 50 and it closes ayah 51. Repetition in the Qur'an is emphasis you can hear. The same seal is pressed on both halves of the message — turn to Him, associate nothing with Him — as if to say: on both of these, the warning has been delivered, plainly, and no one can claim they were not told.

## Living it

The passage does not ask you to admire the universe and stop there. It asks for three things, in order:

**Look, and let it register.** The roof over you was raised without pillars and is protected from falling. The ground under you was spread as a resting place. If your response to that is nothing at all, the ayat have not yet done their work.

**Read the pattern.** Everything you meet comes in pairs — night and day, death and life, Paradise and Fire. The One who made them all is not one of a pair. That is the point, and ayah 49 says so: *that you may remember* — and know that the Creator, Allah, is One without partners.

**Then run.** Ibn Kathir gives you the standing version: seek shelter with Him and trust in Him in all of your affairs. Ibn ʿAbbās gives you the urgent version: flee from your sins and take shelter in Allah for repentance. And Warrāq and Junaid tell you why you cannot afford to stroll — the base self and the devil are both inviting, both deceiving. And when you arrive, arrive with empty hands: no other god set up along with Him. The warner has spoken plainly, twice.

passages.title: Every messenger called sorcerer or madman
passages.tafsir:
These four ayat are a word of comfort to the Prophet ﷺ. Ibn Kathir states the purpose of the passage plainly at its head: **Allah comforts His Prophet ﷺ.** The insults being thrown at him in Makkah are the same words earlier peoples used against their own messengers — and after telling him so, Allah tells him what to do about it: turn away from those who refuse, and keep on reminding.

What holds the passage together is a single movement: **diagnosis** (ayat 52–53 — why they say what they say), then **instruction** (ayat 54–55 — how the Prophet ﷺ is to carry himself in the face of it).

A little earlier in the sūrah, in ayah 50, came the great call *fa-firrū ilā Allāh* — "So flee to Allah." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān records that Sayyidnā Ibn ʿAbbās ؓ explained it as: "Flee from your sins and take shelter in Allah for repentance." Our passage is about what happens when that invitation is refused, and what the one who carries it is to do next.

## Ayah 52 — the oldest insult

> *"Likewise, no Messenger came to those before them but they said: 'A sorcerer or a madman!'"*

Ibn Kathir puts the message of the ayah in Allah's own address to His Messenger ﷺ: *"just as these idolaters denied you, the disbelievers of old used the same words with their Messengers."*

The wording is sweeping. It does not say that some earlier peoples said this, or that many did. It says no messenger came to those before them without this being said to him. Whatever else separated those nations — their languages, their idols, their centuries — the same verdict met the messenger who stood up among them.

**Sorcerer or madman.** *Sāḥir* is the Arabic word rendered "sorcerer"; *majnūn* is the word rendered "madman." Two charges, joined by "or." That is what the Prophet ﷺ was hearing in Makkah, and Allah tells him it is exactly what was heard before him.

The comfort here is not that the words stop hurting. It is that they carry no information about him. They are the old words, and he is standing where every messenger before him stood.

## Ayah 53 — "Have they passed it down to one another?"

> *"Have they transmitted this saying to these? Nay, they are themselves a people transgressing beyond bounds!"*

The question *atawāṣaw bihi* means, as Ibn Kathir glosses it: **"have those of the past taught these words to the people of the present?"** Did the deniers of old leave the Quraysh of Makkah a script to read from — a set of words handed on deliberately from one generation to the next?

It is a question that answers itself, and the ayah answers it in the next breath with *bal* — "nay," "rather":

> *"Nay, they are themselves a people transgressing beyond bounds."*

Ibn Kathir's comment is worth sitting with: **"They are tyrannical people whose hearts are the same. Therefore, the latter said the same as those before them have said."**

That is the diagnosis. *Ṭāghūn* is the word rendered "transgressing beyond bounds" — Ibn Kathir calls such people tyrannical, those who push past the limit Allah set. No chain of transmission was needed. Ibn Kathir traces the identical wording to an identical condition of the heart: because the hearts are the same, the words come out the same.

There is real relief in this for the one being insulted, and Ibn Kathir has already told us that relief is the point of the passage. If the words were a considered response to the man addressed, he would have to examine himself. But the sameness of the words across peoples who never met traces back, in Ibn Kathir's reading, to the state of the ones speaking.

## Ayah 54 — "Turn away from them; you are not blameworthy"

> *"So turn away from them, you are not blameworthy."*

Ibn Kathir glosses *fa-tawalla ʿanhum* directly: **"O Muhammad, turn away from the Quraysh idolaters."** And *fa-mā anta bi-malūm*: **"We blame you not if you turn away from them."**

Feel how tender that second half is. *Malūm* means one who is blamed, reproached, found at fault. Allah does not merely permit the turning away; He states that no reproach attaches to His Messenger ﷺ for it. The permission and the reassurance arrive together, in one ayah, from Allah Himself.

Notice too where the command falls: immediately after the diagnosis of ayah 53. In Ibn Kathir's sequence, the statement that these are people whose hearts have broken past all limits comes first, and *"So turn away from them"* comes next.

Two things this does **not** mean, going by what the sources actually say. It is not a verdict that the Prophet ﷺ failed — Ibn Kathir presents this whole stretch as consolation, not correction. And it is not the end of his mission, because the very next ayah puts him straight back to work.

## Ayah 55 — "And remind"

> *"And remind, for verily, the reminding profits the believers."*

Here is the balance. Ayah 54 says *turn away*; ayah 55 says *and remind*. The two commands are not in tension — they divide the ground. Stop expending yourself on those Allah has just described as transgressing beyond bounds; **do not stop reminding.**

Ibn Kathir's gloss on the second half is exact and slightly bracing: *"for only the believing hearts benefit from being reminded."*

That single sentence redraws the picture of what a caller to Allah is doing.

**First, it tells you where the benefit lands.** *Al-dhikrā* — the reminding — yields its fruit in hearts already alive to Allah. Read this way, turning away from the *ṭāghūn* is no loss at all: they were never the ones in whom the reminder was going to bear fruit. The one who reminds and sees no movement in the mocker has not failed; he has seen the ayah come true in front of him.

**Second, notice who the audience turns out to be.** The passage opens facing the deniers and closes facing *al-muʼminīn*, the believers. The Prophet ﷺ is turned, gently, from the crowd that will not hear toward the people who will.

## Living it

Four things this passage puts in a believer's hands.

**Expect the labels; do not be shaken by them.** Ayah 52 tells you the accusation is older than the accuser. If someone calls the truth you carry manipulation, or calls you unhinged for holding it, you have not met a new argument. You have met the oldest one, and Allah named it to His Messenger ﷺ as comfort.

**Read the insult in the light of what Allah said about the speakers.** Ayah 53 refuses the explanation that the words were handed down; Ibn Kathir traces them instead to hearts that are the same in every generation — tyrannical, past the limit.

**Know when to stop pressing.** Ayah 54 is permission, spoken with reassurance attached: *We blame you not if you turn away from them.* There comes a point where continuing to argue with someone determined not to hear is not perseverance, and Allah says plainly that the one who walks away at that point is not blameworthy. Many believers exhaust themselves in debates Allah never asked them to keep having.

**Never stop reminding.** Ayah 55 keeps the door open on the other side. Turning away from the hostile is not turning away from the work. Keep speaking to the hearts that are alive — including, first of all, your own. And take the ayah's own measure of success with you: the reminding profits the believers. Whether the mocker moves was never the test you were being marked on.

passages.title: Created to worship: the Provider and the wrongdoers' share
passages.tafsir:
These five ayat close Sūrah adh-Dhāriyāt by answering the deepest question a human being can ask — *why do I exist at all?* — and then by settling the account of those who refuse the answer. Allah states the purpose of creation (56), strips away any suggestion that He gains anything from it (57), names Himself as the One who provides rather than the One who is provided for (58), and warns the deniers that their share of punishment is already due and will surely come (59–60).

What holds them together is a single movement: **purpose, then independence, then consequence.** You were made to worship — and the One who made you needs nothing from you, so the worship is entirely for your benefit; refuse it, and the only thing left for you is the portion that fell to those who refused before you.

By way of lead-in, Ibn Kathir places these verses just after a passage of consolation: Allah comforts His Prophet ﷺ that the disbelievers of old used the very same words against their Messengers, tells him to turn away from the Quraysh idolaters without blame, and tells him to keep reminding — "for only the believing hearts benefit from being reminded." That is the doorway into ayah 56. The Prophet ﷺ has been told to stop straining after those who have hardened, and to keep reminding those whose hearts are alive. Now he is told what the whole enterprise is actually for.

## Ayah 56: "I did not create jinn and humans except to worship Me"

Ibn Kathir's gloss is short, and it removes a misunderstanding before it can form: the meaning is *"I, Allah, only created them so that I order them to worship Me, **not that I need them**."* The purpose is a command issued to them, not a lack in Him.

He then quotes the tafsīr of Ibn ʿAbbās, transmitted by ʿAlī bin Abī Talhah, on the words "except that they should worship Me": **"So that they worship Me, willingly or unwillingly."**

Ibn Kathir's summary of the ayah is worth holding onto whole: Allah created the creatures so that they worship Him **alone, without partners**. Those who obey Him will be rewarded with the best rewards; those who disobey Him will receive the worst punishment from Him. Allah has stated that He does not need the creatures — rather **they are in need of Him in all conditions**, since He alone is their Creator and their Provider.

### Two hard questions — and how the scholars answered them

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān pauses here, because the verse's plain wording raises two genuine difficulties.

**First:** if Allah created a creature for a particular task, and it is His will that it perform that task, then rationally it is impossible for that creature to deviate from it — since doing anything contrary to the will of Allah is inconceivable. Yet plainly many jinn and humans do not worship.

**Second:** the purpose of creation seems here restricted to worship alone, whereas there are many other underlying reasons and benefits in the creation of jinn and mankind.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān records that **scholars took different approaches** to these problems, and it is worth noticing that it does not force them into one.

**View one — the verse concerns the believers.** Some say it pertains to the believers only: only believing jinn and believing humans are created for worship and for no other task, and it is obvious that believers are more or less steadfast in worship. This is reported as the view of **Dahhāk, Sufyān Thawrī and others**. Maʿārif adds that according to one version from **Sayyidnā Ibn ʿAbbās (may Allah be pleased with him)**, the word *muʼminīn* ("the believers") occurs in the verse itself — "And I have not created the **believing** jinn and mankind except that they should worship Me" — a version which supports this reading.

**View two — command plus free will.** Maʿārif gives the answer of **Moulānā Ashraf ʿAlī Thānawī (may Allah have mercy on him)**: Allah has commanded all to worship, and at the same time has equipped them with free will. Some exercised that Allah-given free will correctly and chose to worship Him; others used it incorrectly and deviated from worshipping Him. Maʿārif notes this is what **Sayyidnā ʿAlī (may Allah be pleased with him)** said, as quoted by **Baghawī**. In other words, the verse states the purpose for which we were made and commanded — not a compulsion that removes the choice.

**View three — the innate capacity.** **Tafsīr Mazharī** offers what Maʿārif calls a plain and simple explication: Allah has equipped every jinn and every human with the **innate capacity** to worship. Some use that capacity rightly and succeed; others employ it wrongly, in sinning and in fulfilling their base emotions, and thus destroy it.

Maʿārif grounds this in the teaching reported from the Messenger ﷺ that **every child is born according to the *fitrah***, and that it is his parents who cause him to deviate from that unadulterated propensity and turn him into a Jew, a Christian, or a Magian. According to the majority of the scholars, *fitrah* here refers to the religion of Islam. The parallel is exact: just as every man is born with the natural capacity for Islam and true faith, and it is his parents who adulterate and destroy that capacity and put him on to the ways of disbelief — so "except that they should worship Me" could mean that **every member of jinn and mankind has the natural, inborn capacity to worship.** Maʿārif closes the discussion the way a careful scholar should: *Allah, the Pure and Exalted, knows best.*

**And the second question** — the apparent narrowing of human purpose to worship alone — Maʿārif answers briefly and sensibly: bringing any creation into being for the purpose of worship **does not necessarily imply that they are unfit for other functions of life.** Work, family, trade, learning, governance — none of these is excluded. Worship is the purpose that gives the rest its meaning, not a replacement for the rest.

## Ayah 57: "I seek no provision from them, nor do I need them to feed Me"

If worship is the purpose, the obvious human instinct is to imagine that Allah somehow *gains* from it. Ayah 57 shuts that door.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān unpacks it with an image drawn from how people actually think. The verse, it says, means that by creating jinn and mankind Allah does not stand in need of them — not so that they should produce sustenance for Him, nor for themselves, nor for any of His other creations, nor that they should earn to feed Him. And it notes that this is stated "according to the general trend of people": **the most affluent of men buys a slave and spends on him not for nothing**, but with an underlying purpose — he expects the slave to work for him, help him in his tasks, fulfil his needs, and earn a livelihood for his master. That is how ownership works among human beings. **Allah is immaculate, pure and above all these things.** In creating human beings, Maʿārif states plainly, He does not profit or benefit anything.

This is the hinge of the whole passage. Worship is not a tax Allah collects. It is the one activity in which the entire benefit flows toward the worshipper.

## Ayah 58: The Provider, Owner of power, the Most Strong

Having denied that He receives provision, Allah names Himself by the opposite: *"Indeed, Allah alone is the Supreme Provider — Lord of all Power, the Most Strong."*

Ibn Kathir records here that **Imam Ahmad** reported from **ʿAbdullāh bin Masʿūd** that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ taught the wording in the first person — *"Verily, I am the Provider, Owner of power, the Most Strong."* Ibn Kathir notes that **Abū Dāwūd, At-Tirmidhī and An-Nasāʼī** also collected this hadith, and that **At-Tirmidhī said: "Hasan Sahih."** The force of it is to put the declaration directly in the mouth of the One being spoken about: the same "I" who said *I did not create them except to worship Me* and *I seek no provision from them* now says *I am the Provider.*

**From the Sunnah — worship and the filling of the heart.** Ibn Kathir then brings a hadith that turns this doctrine into daily experience. **Imam Ahmad** recorded that **Abū Hurayrah** said that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said that Allah the Exalted said:

> "O Son of Adam! Busy yourself in worshipping Me, and I will fill your chest with riches and dissipate your meekness. Otherwise, I will fill your chest with distracting affairs and will not do away with your meekness."

Ibn Kathir notes that **At-Tirmidhī and Ibn Mājah** collected this hadith, and that **At-Tirmidhī said: "Hasan Gharīb."**

Read it beside ayah 57 and the logic lands. Allah gains nothing from your worship — but *you* gain the thing every human being is chasing: a chest filled with riches instead of a chest filled with distracting affairs. The alternative is not freedom from service; it is a crowded heart, with the neediness still not lifted.

## Ayah 59: the bucket at the well

Now the passage turns to those who refuse. "The wrongdoers will certainly have a share ˹of the torment˺" — like the share of their companions.

The Arabic word is **ذَنُوب — *dhanūb***, and Maʿārif ul Qurʼān opens it up beautifully. It means **a large bucket kept at the common wells of a locality** for the purpose of drawing and filling water. Where a village shares one well and one great bucket, **a turn is designated** for each of the people using it, so that when his turn comes he is conveniently able to fill his own private bucket. From that everyday scene the word comes to be employed in the sense of **turn, share or portion**. Hence Maʿārif's rendering: *"So, those who did wrong deserve a share (in the punishment) like the share of their companions."*

The image is worth sitting with. Punishment here is not chaos; it is a queue at a well, where each has his designated turn and his share.

Maʿārif draws out the warning precisely: **the past communities were given an opportunity to work.** When each of those communities did not take advantage of the opportunity in its own time and persisted in its evil course, they were punished and destroyed. Likewise, the present pagans of Makkah are **designated a time and opportunity**. If they do not take advantage of the allocated time and opportunity and persist in their paganism, they will be punished in this world; otherwise the punishment of the Hereafter is most certain. They will meet a fate similar to that of the opponents of the former Prophets, and like them come to a sad end.

**"So let them not ask Me to hasten on."** Ibn Kathir explains this closing clause of ayah 59 simply: the wrongdoers will receive their due share of the torment, so let them not ask that the punishment be rushed to them — **for it will surely come.** Maʿārif says the same: their due share will surely come in due time, so they should not ask for it to be hastened. Delay is not absence. Their turn has merely not yet arrived.

## Ayah 60: the last word of the sūrah

"Woe then to the disbelievers when they face their Day which they have been promised." Ibn Kathir identifies that Day in one phrase: **the Day of Resurrection.**

Notice how the sūrah ends. Not with the punishment of a particular tribe, and not with a worldly reckoning, but with the promised Day itself — the appointment none of them can renegotiate.

## Living it

- **Your purpose is not something you must invent.** Ayah 56 has already told you what you were made for. Every other good thing in life — work, family, learning — sits inside that purpose rather than competing with it; as Maʿārif ul Qurʼān says, being created for worship does not necessarily imply that a person is unfit for other functions of life.
- **Worship costs Allah nothing and profits you everything.** Ayah 57 removes any thought that you are doing Allah a favour, and the master-and-slave comparison in Maʿārif makes the contrast vivid: unlike every human master, He does not profit or benefit anything from those He creates.
- **Anxiety about provision is misplaced.** Ayah 58 names Allah the All-Provider, Owner of power, the Most Strong. The hadith of Ibn Masʿūd puts that in the first person; the hadith of Abū Hurayrah tells you what becomes of the chest that turns toward Him and the chest that turns away.
- **The capacity is already in you.** On Tafsīr Mazharī's reading, you were equipped with the innate capacity to worship — the question is whether you use it rightly or employ it wrongly until it is destroyed.
- **Do not mistake delay for safety.** Ayah 59 says the share is due and will surely come; ayah 60 names the Day. Time given is opportunity, not exemption — which is exactly how Maʿārif ul Qurʼān read the warning to the Makkans.

*And Allah knows best.*
